0.beginner: The classic "leave home, wander, come back" story — you hear it in almost every song.
0.learner: The T-S-D-T functional loop, a perfect cadence; the key has never been clearer.
0.pro: Authentic cadence; watch the V7 third/seventh resolution and the preparation of the cadential six-four.

1.beginner: The three building blocks jazz uses most: prepare, push, come home.
1.learner: ii7-V7-Imaj7, the core grammar of the shortest guide-tone connections.
1.pro: ii-V-I; focus on 3/7 voice leading, alt tensions, and the tritone sub.

2.beginner: The minor-key version of prepare, push, come home — darker colors, more drama.
2.learner: iiø7-V7alt-imMaj7, a strong resolution in minor.
2.pro: Minor ii-V-i; V7alt takes the altered scale, and i can be mMaj7/6/9.

3.beginner: The smoothest loop for a chorus — the emotional rise and fall lands just right.
3.learner: I-V-vi-IV: stable and singable, made for choruses.
3.pro: Pop axis; can rotate to vi-IV-I-V — mind the bass line and the hook.

4.beginner: Swap the usual dominant for a distant cousin chord, and the bass slides down by a half step.
4.learner: bII7 shares its tritone with V7, and the bass resolves down a half step.
4.pro: Tritone sub; Lydian Dominant works over bII7, where #11 is the color tone.

5.beginner: Borrow two chords from the parallel minor and the picture suddenly turns cinematic.
5.learner: Modal interchange: bVI/bVII borrowed from the parallel minor.
5.pro: Modal interchange; watch the parallel major triads of bVI-bVII-I and the voice leading.

beginner.body: Think of writing an essay: state the theme, leave it, then come home. Classical harmony is just writing that "coming home" route clearly.
points: Find the tonic first — that is home
Use IV and V to create the feeling of leaving and wanting to return
Let every voice leap as little as possible and move smoothly

learner.body: Built around key, cadence, passing harmony, and voice leading; tonic, dominant, and subdominant build a clear structure.
points: The I-IV-V-I functional loop
Resolution of neighbor tones, passing tones, and suspensions
Avoiding parallel fifths and octaves in four-part writing

pro.body: The syntax layer of functional harmony: cadences, passing six-four chords, Neapolitan and augmented sixths, pedals, and voice engineering.
points: Perfect/plagal/deceptive/imperfect cadences
Preparation and resolution of N6 and It/Fr/Ger+6
Bass line, inner voices, and harmonic rhythm

beginner.body: Jazz chords sound "thick" because sevenths and ninths sit on top of the triad. Grab the third and seventh first and you will not get lost.
points: ii-V-I is the three building blocks you will use most
The third and seventh define the chord's character
The fifth can usually be left out

learner.body: Built around functional harmony, substitute dominants, guide tones, and minimal voice movement; third and seventh first, then add tensions.
points: The core grammar of ii-V-I
Omitting the fifth keeps the voices clearer
When to use alt, sus, and upper structures

pro.body: Treat ii-V-I as a swappable syntactic unit: tritone sub, modal interchange, upper-structure triads, and chord-scale choices.
points: Guide-tone lines and 3/7 resolution
Choosing between V7alt / Lydian Dominant / Whole-tone
Drop 2/3 versus rootless — the arranging trade-off

beginner.body: A mode is the same set of notes with a different "home". Move the home and the whole color of the music changes with it.
points: First hear where the tonic is
Compare whether the third is major or minor
Remember one note that makes it distinctive

learner.body: When switching between major, minor, harmonic minor, and melodic minor, lock the tonic first, then identify the third and seventh.
points: Listen for the tonal center first
Compare major and minor thirds and sevenths
Practice parallel modes on the same tonic

pro.body: Treat modes as a chord-to-scale mapping system: characteristic notes set the color, avoid notes set the resolution, and upper structures set the voicing.
points: Quick judgment of characteristic versus avoid notes
Parallel modal interchange and borrowed chords
Voicing modal vamps and pedal points

beginner.body: The keyboard works in three layers: bass in the left hand, chords in the middle, melody in the right. On guitar, start by making sure it is playable and clear.
points: Do not let the bass get too thick
Save the melody for the right hand
Drop the fifth whenever you can

learner.body: Keyboard layers: bass and skeleton in the left hand, melody and upper structures in the right; guitar favors playable shapes and clear voices.
points: Separate bass and inner voices by register
Keep the melody and guide tones
Position beats playing every note

pro.body: Arranging is the distribution of space and function: low end for the bass, midrange for 3/7 and tensions, high end for color and melody.
points: Dividing the work between rootless voicings and the bass
Drop 2/3 and two-hand distribution
Tension density and the rhythm of resolution

historyIntro.beginner: No need to memorize dates — treat it as one storyline of music becoming freer: from single-line chant, to functional harmony, to jazz and pop.
historyIntro.learner: From Greek ratios, church modes, major/minor, and figured bass to chromaticism, the modal revival, and jazz grammar — understand the "why" of each stage.
historyIntro.pro: The coupled evolution of tuning systems, notation, and harmonic syntax: how twelve-tone equal temperament unlocked modulation, how functional harmony was dismantled by chromaticism and modal thinking, and how it reassembled in jazz and pop.
